summary:
Two phrases are scrambles exactly when they have the same letter counts, after dropping spaces and ignoring
case. Count with 26 counters: +1 for each letter of `a`, −1 for each letter of `b`; every counter must end at 0.
O(n + m).

question.md:
Ignoring spaces and case, does `b` use exactly the same letters as `a`, the same number of times?

- **Spaces don't count**, and lengths with spaces may differ.
- **Up to 10⁵ characters each.**

think.md:
`"Dormitory"` and `"dirty room"` both reduce to the letters d, i, m, o, o, r, r, t, y: **true**.

Order doesn't matter, only how many of each letter. That's a signature: sorted letters, or 26 counts. Counts
are cheaper.

idea.md: Lowercase, drop spaces, sort both, compare.

lines.text: Lowercase letters without spaces, sorted: a canonical form.
Scrambles have the same canonical form.

walk.title: Normalise both phrases (drop spaces, lowercase), sort the letters, and compare.

limits.md: Sorting does more than needed. Only the letter counts matter, and 26 counters give them in linear time.

idea.md: `cnt[letter] += 1` over `a`, `−= 1` over `b` (skipping spaces, folding case). True if all counts are 0.

lines.text: Letters of `a` add, letters of `b` subtract; spaces skipped, case folded.

walk.title: 26 counters: add 1 for every letter of a, subtract 1 for every letter of b. Scrambles leave every counter at zero.

takeaways.md:
- **Anagram test = equal letter counts.** One counter array: add for one string, subtract for the other.
- Normalise first (case, spaces) so the signature captures exactly what "same" means.
- Sorting works too, at O(n log n).
